title: Two routes to CO₂
hook: Burn carbon in one step or two. Does taking the detour change the heat you get?

knows: that bond energies set reaction heat (pay-first-then-profit)
doesNotKnow: that the total heat of a reaction does not depend on the route, so steps add up to the direct value

misconception: A reaction done in two steps releases more heat in total (two fires) or less (energy lost in between) than the same reaction done directly.
objective: The learner can say that burning carbon to CO2 releases 393.51 kJ/mol by any route, and explain that heat depends only on the start and end states, so measured steps can be added to find a reaction's heat.

claims.text: The standard enthalpy of formation of CO2(g) is −393.51 kJ/mol and of CO(g) −110.53 kJ/mol, so burning carbon (graphite) to CO2 releases 393.51 kJ/mol and to CO 110.53 kJ/mol (stage step labels '−393.51', '−110.53', end level 'CO₂', sums 'Σ −393.51'; reveal: '−393.51 kJ per mole of CO₂', 'carbon monoxide (−110.53 ...').
claims.source: CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics (Cox, Wagman & Medvedev, 1989): ΔfH CO2(g) −393.51 ± 0.13, CO(g) −110.53 ± 0.17 kJ/mol; CRC Handbook, standard thermodynamic properties of chemical substances. Brief claim 1.

claims.text: Burning CO to CO2 releases about 282.98 kJ/mol (stage step label '−282.98'; reveal: 'then −282.98').
claims.source: Hess's law from claim 1: −393.51 − (−110.53) = −282.98 kJ/mol (node, demo-builder 2026-10-14). Demo.tsx steps('co'). Brief claim 2.

claims.text: Turning graphite into diamond takes about +1.90 kJ/mol, so burning diamond to CO2 releases about 395.41 kJ/mol (stage step labels '+1.90 diamond', '−395.41'; reveal: 'climbed +1.90 to diamond first').
claims.source: CRC Handbook, standard thermodynamic properties (ΔfH C(diamond) = 1.9 kJ/mol); NBS tables (Wagman et al., 1982) 1.895 kJ/mol. −393.51 − 1.90 = −395.41 (node). Drawing note: on the ladder 1.9 kJ is under 1 px, so the diamond level is drawn 3 px above the start level (Demo.tsx YDIA); the number label carries the size. Brief claim 3.

claims.text: Heat released depends only on where you start and where you finish (enthalpy is a state function: Hess's law), so chemists add measured steps to find the heat of reactions they cannot measure directly (reveal; stage: all three sums 'Σ −393.51').
claims.source: Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, thermochemistry (Hess's law; enthalpy as a state function); the three sums on the stage, each added from its own steps in Demo.tsx sumOf(). The CO case is the textbook example: the heat of C + ½O2 → CO is hard to measure directly because some CO2 always forms (Atkins). Brief claim 4.

claims.text: Model disclosure: the routes are bookkeeping. Carbon burning in air makes a mixture; the stage shows each step as if it went to completion, at standard conditions (25 °C, 1 bar).
claims.source: The lesson's own simplification (brief claim 5); not shown on the stage (text budget).

claims.text: Like height lost walking downhill by any path (reveal).
claims.source: Analogy: gravitational potential energy is also a state function of position; the analogy claims only path independence.

recall.question: Step 1 of a reaction releases 50 kJ and step 2 absorbs 20 kJ. The same overall reaction done in one step releases how much?
options: It depends on how fast it is done
recall.why: Heat depends only on the start and end, so the one-step route releases the sum of the steps: 50 − 20 = 30 kJ (Hess's law).
